Thank you, Mr. Chair. This information report provides an update on animal cruelty investigations in Saskatoon. And just as a reminder, the animal cruelty investigations are animal protection is under the animal protection act, which is provincial legislation.

And while the city has no direct role in the provision of these services administration has been working collaboratively with the various parties to ensure the provision of animal protection services is indeed available within Saskatoon.
Once the SPCA discontinued the provision of this service on March 31, 2022, the Saskatoon police started to monitor impact of call for services relative to animal welfare or animal protection.
And since July 1, 2022, animal cruelty investigation services in Saskatoon are being provided through the Ministry of Agriculture by the animal protection services Saskatoon.
They provide services between the hours of 80 m and 5 p.m. Monday to Friday. The police is then typically a first point of contact for response.
For after hour calls, regarding concerns for animal neglect, harm or endangerment.
For the period of April to December 31 of 2022, the Saskatoon police logged a total of 228 calls for service.
And of all the calls received, as shown on page two of this report, only two of them were indeed confirmed or suspected cases of animal cruelty that required the police to respond.
Administration is appreciative the Ministry is now supporting the provision of animal protection services in Saskatoon, where they had previously provided no service level.

Following the transition to a new service model by APSS in July of 2022, administration and police reached out to the Ministry to explore options to provide enforcement beyond the current hours of service.

The Ministry confirmed animal cruelty concerns outside the current APSS operating hours. If there was additional service required by a city for its residents, the responsibility would be for the local government.

To assist in the overall continuing of care, administration negotiated an agreement with SPCA for 2023 to accept animals from police, the ones that are seized under the animal protection act, so that the animals can be accepted after hours and on weekends.
And the administration also worked with the Saskatoon animal control agency to assist in the transportation of any animal seized by police.
Then going forward, beginning in 2024, the new animal services contracts for both animals by law services and pound services will include the services and the costs associated with this work.

So administration was asked to report back on several items related to provisions in the zoning by law.
Related to shelters, including the newest regulations that provide for an emergency residential shelter as a temporary use only.
As well as possible changes concerning on site outdoor space requirements for future shelter facilities and requirements for the approval process.
So as background, Saskton has had shelters of various types for many years.
Which have been classified as various uses under the zoning by law,
according to how each shelter was being operated and considering when it was applied for because many of them go back many years.
We currently have five facilities in operation providing shelter services in all of them are permanent and legally operating.
The city has never had a definition of shelter.
You know, the actual term shelter in our zoning by law prior to the amendments to define an emergency residential shelter,
which was approved in 2021.
The main reason for incorporating that definition at that time and the associated approval process was to provide for an emergency residential shelter as a temporary use on an urgent basis.
So it was key that that's a temporary use.
In 2021, those new provisions were added and this created a path for administrative approval to address life's safety requirements,
technical considerations and operational plans for a temporary use.
These considerations were identified as the critical pieces that needed to be addressed,
recognizing that establishing a new temporary facility could be required on an urgent basis.
The current approval process that we have in place provided a streamlined path for a temporary use.
This approval process could be changed and could require city council approval instead.
This would extend the timeline but would create an opportunity for public comment to city council through that process.
In terms of communication and consultation processes for the temporary use,
when we developed the current regulations for the temporary facilities,
administration developed the streamlined approval process as noted,
recognizing the urgent need for the facility to be able to come on stream in advance of winter.
The focus of the regulations was an ensuring life safety for occupants of the temporary facility,
as such, no requirements for consultation or communication were embedded in the requirements.
Communication and consultation could be added to the process and we've laid out two options for this approach.
One option would add a notification process to the current administrative approval,
and comments received through that would be reviewed, administration would work with the applicant to mitigate the concerns as appropriate.
The second option proposed would be in the case of a change to the approval process to include approval by city council.
This again would be a notification process and administration would review any correspondence received and would work with the applicant to mitigate concerns.
Any correspondence received would then be compiled for city council to consider,
and when city council considers the information and the application speakers and correspondence could of course be received at that time as well.
In both cases, this option that we have put forward is a notification process and not an engagement process.
In addition, in order to manage resources, individual correspondence received by administration through either option,
would not receive detailed individual responses.
To add to this service level would require additional resourcing or would further impact the service levels to other development applications that we have in process at the same time.
For a permanent facility, if we receive an application for a new permanent shelter type facility,
it will need to meet zoning regulations and the building code requirements of a full permanent use.
If the proposed site that the applicant is considering allows for the use as a permitted use, it will be processed as such by administration.
Similar to how all other permitted uses are administered, there is no communication notification or consultation during that process.
The applicant applies for a building and development permit if they meet a requirements it's approved.

If it is not a permitted use on the proposed site, it would then require either rezoning or discretionary use process, which would then follow the typical approach, including consultation, review by municipal planning commission and a public hearing and city council.
In terms of the request for considering onsite amenity space for the temporary emergency residential shelter, a request was made through this committee to consider that.
The proposal for onsite amenity space is I think a good one, it could accommodate a variety of types of spaces and would be beneficial to the occupants of the facilities.
It would be ideal if this could be accommodated at any site.
However, finding an appropriate site would be further limited if we add detailed requirements for this type of space to our current regulations.
Reflecting on the process in 2021, the applicant looked at many sites and had difficulties securing an appropriate site for a temporary use.
Further limiting the potential sites by adding additional bailout requirements may make an already difficult search even harder.
An alternative would be to create a set of guidelines or considerations to share with any future applicants.
These would not be regulatory or enforceable, but would be a method to outline items for them to consider.
For a permanent facility on the other hand, onsite amenity space is already required for all uses in the zoning bylaw and would be required to be required to be met in order to receive approval.

So in summary, at this time, the administration is not recommending changes, but welcomes any direction from committee in regards to the changes to the requirements or process that we've outlined in this report.
